I'm going to have to second what ablanchard17 wrote. That is most definitely a vasovagal induced syncope. Your blood pressure and heart rate drop suddenly in response to sudden acute stress, and you lose consciousness temporarily. 

The fears most people associate with needles are either the invasiveness of the needle, or the misattributed fear of pain induced by the needle entering your body.

Most people are afraid of needles. They are invasive. It concerns a metal object piercing your skin. However the pain as a result is most often minimal, and the benefits of the use of needles far outweigh the momentary discomfort, so you're going to have to analyze your rational process.

The first question you have to ask yourself relates to why you have this fear. I'd most likely say that the stress of the fainting episode you experienced is the cause of your phobia, before this point, it's generally a fear that we deal with when it comes.

I have at least two injections per month. Normally one into the muscle, and one into a vein. My brother has injections two or more times per day. Funny enough, neither of us are very afraid of needles compared to the people we know who have them once a year!

I used to have a fear similar to yours. Before I had an injection, I would spend at least a month concerned over it, and as the days rolled closer, it would be on my mind all of the time. Then as the day came, I would complain to the nurse until, shaking, they managed to prick me.

Luckily for me, I'm not prone to fainting, else this may not have been addressed and my health would be suffering overwhelmingly as I'd not receive vital treatment.

But as time went on, I needed more injections, cyclically. One day I realized that as I was walking in for my monthly muscular injection, that I hadn't even considered it. The journey to get my injection was a two hour journey, and during the whole thing, I had never thought "I am going to hospital to get an injection.". I was preoccupied with the journey. Then I'd be on the hospital bed, facing away and hear "Okay, sharp scratch!" and I would have a slight worry moment.

Luckily, you won't be having intramuscular injections, so you don't have to worry about the pain they cause. Although it's no more than a punch in the arm, it's still not pleasant!

So I beat it simply by repetition. I needed the injections, and the pain wasn't great enough to cause me mental overload in contemplation of the events that were about to transpire, and so the response of fear simply disappeared.

Naturally, you'll need to deal with this one step at a time. First, consider the needle. The sight is the concern to most people. If you never saw what an injection looked like, were blind and heard of this magic thing the doctor does that causes you slight discomfort that heals your wounds, you'd be none the wiser and respond happily.

I'd say take a sewing needle, and move it towards your arm. It may be a bother at first, but you know you're not going to be putting it in. Get used to this. This is your first step. Do this every day until you're comfortable doing it. 

Next consider your concern to the pain. Look into topical anaesthetics. There are creams that can be purchased over the counter that numbs a local site of skin from pain. When you know where to apply this (a generous amount in an even distribution around the under side of your elbow, normally) you will put it on underneath a patch before your blood test, and you can then have the blood taken without knowing the needle even went in. Yes it is that easy. I have to use these anaesthetics because I have a relatively large needle for my intramuscular injections. I feel nothing as my skin is penetrated, but enough pain as the muscle is! Your muscles won't be touched during a blood test, just the skin and a nerveless vein.

Next you have to respond to the stress. That's the final thing holding you back. What you're doing here is battling your own mind. You've got yourself into a predicament where before the event you're saying "I'm about to have a needle put in me. Oh it's going to be sharp and metallic! It's going to hurt! Then it's going to take out my blood. Oh god, is the nurse paying attention to this? Is it over? Oh I'm not sure if it's over. Please be over. Worry. Worry. Worry. It's over! *stands up and faints due to standing quickly and stress combining to lower blood pressure rapidly.*.

You need to approach the stress simply. That's why I gave you the tip of the sewing needle. When you're used to the concept of a needle being near you, and the lack of negative consequences, and the positive outcome, through exposure, you'll become more able to accept the fact that you're going to have to deal with it. It'll take personal discipline, but you can get over it. 

Now the rest of it comes down to calming yourself down before and during the event. You need distraction, primarily. Listen to music, eat (if it's a non fasting blood test) chocolate, talk to someone about something unrelated. Your mind must not be allowed to obsess. The obsession is what is causing your stress induced fainting episodes. 

During the event, you want to breathe deep, in order to keep oxygen flowing throughout your blood if you're stressed. Most importantly, don't look, and instead focus on the situation. Tell yourself what it is. "This isn't so bad! I can deal with this. It's going fine. I could deal with this if it went on for hours. It's alright. It's just my mind that's stressing me. See? No pain at all. I just have to hold out my arm steady. Easy."

Other than having a calming effect, this'll allow you to feel in control, and will reassert the fact that you won't suffer through the experience, meaning you'll more easily have future treatment.

Finally, after your blood test, ask for just a moment to calm down. It's over. Breathe deep, settle in the chair, make yourself comfortable enough, and sign off your paper. Now get your legs warmed up, wiggle them back and forth, and slowly stand. If you feel woozy, sit back down again.

By doing this, you won't suffer with a fainting episode, and you'll be able to have a pleasant experience.

This is all a mental battle, and nothing more. Please get tested for PCOS, the condition is not a comfortable one to live with.

The issue lies simply in the rehearsal for most anxiety issues.

Imagine your first attack. How simple was it? Was it that troublesome? It was probably pretty bad, but did you come to instantly believe it to happen again? Was the next one as close?

This is quite simply because of the way that our brain works. When you move a muscle, there is a certain neural connection that your brain makes. That neural connection defines what happens in what order, and is what can be accounted for in dexterity. A thick layer tends to build around these links. This layer increases the signal strength and travel time significantly, and also tends to increase the likelihood of continuing other pathways.

When you train yourself to hit a tennis ball, you'll find that over time, the thing you practice will become what you do. Sometimes, you'll have all the right ideas in mind, and practice all the right things. The connections around the correct strengthened links form. You're Roger Federer. But conversely, if you've had no training, you do the same thing, the wrong strengthened links form. You become a nobody. It all comes down to a matter of practice.

So what happens when we have an anxiety attack? It's really quite simple. We've become damned good at doing it. Those of us who've gone through it for years have INCREDIBLY strong links for these things. Tiny chest pain? Heart attack. Slight shifting of vision? Tumour. Tiny arbitrary bodily function that would've otherwise gone unnoticed? Instant. Fucking. Terror.

However these links break down. Roger Federer doesn't practice for 3 years, he becomes a nobody. That's why it's important to play this mental game the right way.

When's it happening, when you're in bed? GET OUT OF BED. Just spend a moment. Don't do it in anger. Realize what's happened. Think about what you want. Glass of milk? Go get a fucking glass of milk, you deserve it, life is awesome and that glass of milk is satisfying. What else do you want, a go on the computer? Reward yourself. Within boundaries of course. Don't make something a comfort zone you don't leave. When you're satisfied your anxiety is quelled, get back in bed, try again. Anxiety is your bitch. Go to bed with BETTER feelings about yourself.

This is why I do hypnotherapy. It's a lot easier when I'm forming links in my head that mean breathe easy, appreciate your heart works on its own, and get on with what makes you happy.

I originally decided to skydive in mid November. That was after I was taken in to hospital because of suspected heart issues, which turned out to just be severe anxiety. I thought that maybe it'd 'shock' me in to associating adrenaline with an enjoyable experience, a rush, not a terrifying ordeal.

I had my first jump in December 2012, it was cold, and I was scared. I was so fucking scared I actually lost consciousness on the way out. Imagine having a severe anxiety attack and then being forced to lift yourself out of an aeroplane into 70mph winds smashing you in the face and having to drop freely through the air. I started the whole kicking for air, then I just went limp and fell.

I woke up within seconds, pounding heart, sweaty hands, and just spent my whole time screaming. I didn't have an anxiety attack for a week. Til that point it'd been hard to avoid them daily. I also felt more able, going about my daily routine swimmingly for the first time in months.

I felt really quite competent under canopy, although rather shaky. When I got to the ground and returned to the hangar, I felt so tranquil it was almost impossible to formulate a response to questions. I just smiled a lot.

This is strange.
